{{short description|Generalization of the Levi-Civita connection}}
In [[differential geometry]], a '''Weyl connection''' (also called a '''Weyl structure''') is a generalization of the [[Levi-Civita connection]] that makes sense on a [[conformal manifold]].  They were introduced by [[Hermann Weyl]] {{harv|Weyl|1918}} in an attempt to unify general relativity and electromagnetism.  His approach, although it did not lead to a successful theory,<ref>{{harvnb|Bergmann|1942|loc=Chapter XVI: Weyl's gauge-invariant geometry}}</ref> lead to further developments of the theory in [[conformal geometry]], including a detailed study by [[Élie Cartan]] {{harv|Cartan|1943}}.  They were also discussed in {{harvtxt|Eisenhart|1927}}.

Specifically, let <math>M</math> be a smooth manifold, and <math>[g]</math> a conformal class of (non-degenerate) [[metric tensor]]s on <math>M</math>, where <math>h,g\in[g]</math> iff <math>h=e^{2\gamma}g</math> for some smooth function <math>\gamma</math> (see [[Weyl transformation]]).  A Weyl connection is a torsion free [[affine connection]] on <math>M</math> such that, for any <math>g\in [g]</math>,
<math display="block">\nabla g = \alpha_g \otimes g</math>
where <math>\alpha_g</math> is a one-form depending on <math>g</math>.  

If <math>\nabla</math> is a Weyl connection and <math>h=e^{2\gamma}g</math>, then
<math display="inline">\nabla h = (2\,d\gamma+\alpha_g)\otimes h</math>
so the one-form transforms by 
<math display="inline">\alpha_{e^{2\gamma}g} = 2\,d\gamma+\alpha_g.</math>
Thus the notion of a Weyl connection is conformally invariant, and the change in one-form is mediated by a [[de Rham cohomology|de Rham cocycle]].

An example of a Weyl connection is the Levi-Civita connection for any metric in the conformal class <math>[g]</math>, with <math>\alpha_g=0</math>.  This is not the most general case, however, as any such Weyl connection has the property that the one-form <math>\alpha_h</math> is closed for all <math>h</math> belonging to the conformal class.  In general, the [[Ricci curvature]] of a Weyl connection is not symmetric.  Its skew part is the dimension times the two-form <math>d\alpha_g</math>, which is independent of <math>g</math> in the conformal class, because the difference between two <math>\alpha_g</math> is a de Rham cocycle.  Thus, by the [[Poincaré lemma]], the Ricci curvature is symmetric if and only if the Weyl connection is locally the Levi-Civita connection of some element of the conformal class.<ref>{{harvnb|Higa|1993}}</ref>

Weyl's original hope was that the form <math>\alpha_g</math> could represent the [[vector potential]] of electromagnetism (a gauge dependent quantity), and <math>d\alpha_g</math> the field strength (a gauge invariant quantity). This synthesis is unsuccessful in part because the [[gauge group]] is wrong: electromagnetism is associated with a <math>U(1)</math> gauge field, not an <math>\mathbb R</math> gauge field.

{{harvtxt|Hall|1992}} showed that an affine connection is a Weyl connection if and only if its [[holonomy group]] is a subgroup of the [[conformal group]].  The possible holonomy algebras in Lorentzian signature were analyzed in {{harvtxt|Dikarev|2021}}. 

A '''Weyl manifold''' is a manifold admitting a global Weyl connection.  The global analysis of Weyl manifolds is actively being studied.  For example, {{harvtxt|LeBrun|Mason|2009}} considered complete Weyl manifolds such that the [[Einstein equations|Einstein vacuum equations]] hold, an [[Einstein–Weyl geometry]], obtaining a complete characterization in three dimensions.

Weyl connections also have current applications in [[string theory]] and [[holographic principle|holography]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Ciambelli|Leigh|2020}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Jia|Karydas|2021}}</ref>

Weyl connections have been generalized to the setting of [[parabolic geometry (differential geometry)|parabolic geometries]], of which conformal geometry is a special case, in {{harvtxt|Čap|Slovák|2003}}.
